cases.description: Microsoft's first documented worked example: inverse of the left-tailed chi-squared probability 0.93 at 1 degree of freedom
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 3.283020286, which is a TRUNCATION rather than a rounding of the true value. Independently derived from the documented left-tail inverse: scipy.stats.chi2.ppf(0.93, 1) = 3.283020286759539, whose correct 9-decimal rounding is 3.283020287, not the published 3.283020286. Asserting at 8 dp (3.28302029) is the deepest precision at which the published figure and the mathematically correct value agree, so this case tests the function rather than the page's truncation

cases.description: Microsoft's second documented worked example: inverse of the left-tailed chi-squared probability 0.6 at 2 degrees of freedom
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 1.832581464. Independently derived two ways: scipy.stats.chi2.ppf(0.6, 2) = 1.83258146374831, and in closed form, since the chi-squared distribution with 2 degrees of freedom is exponential with mean 2, the inverse is -2*ln(1-0.6) = -2*ln(0.4) = 1.83258146374831 -> 1.832581464 at 9 dp

cases.description: A non-integer degrees-of-freedom argument, which the documentation says is truncated
cases.expected_note: Excel documents "If deg_freedom is not an integer, it is truncated", so 2.9 must behave exactly as 2 and return the documented 1.832581464. Independently checked that this discriminates: a genuine 2.9 degrees of freedom would give chi2.ppf(0.6, 2.9) = 2.835555
Excel documents: "If probability < 0 or probability > 1, CHISQ.INV returns the #NUM! error value."
Excel documents: "If deg_freedom < 1 or deg_freedom > 10^10, CHISQ.INV returns the #NUM! error value."
Excel documents: "If argument is nonnumeric, CHISQ.INV returns the #VALUE! error value."
